Churchland et al. (2010) on dandiset 000140 (MC_Maze_Small)¶

Paper. Churchland MM, Cunningham JP, Kaufman MT, Ryu SI, Shenoy KV (2010). Cortical preparatory activity: representation of movement or first cog in a dynamical machine? Neuron 68:387-400, doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2010.09.015.

Claims. claims/000140/10.1016-j.neuron.2010.09.015.yaml, written from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC2991102) and its supplement (NIHMS240235-supplement-01.pdf), and checked by a second reader. The claims file decides what is tested; method details it lacks are taken from the paper and cited where they are used, here and in maze_prep.py.

Dataset. DANDI:000140, version 0.220113.0408 (doi:10.48324/dandi.000140/0.220113.0408), streamed. The paper cites no version of the dandiset. 0.220113.0408 is the only published version; the draft (modified 2023-06-20) has the same two assets and size. A published version is fixed, so it is pinned.

The dandiset is the Neural Latents Benchmark's MC_Maze_Small: one session of monkey J (Jenkins, 2009-09-28) with two 96-electrode arrays, 100 train/val trials over 27 maze conditions, and 100 test segments without conditions. The paper's J-array dataset has 108 conditions and 2166 trials per neuron; the dandiset holds 27 of its conditions (or of a session like it) with 1 to 4 analysable trials each. The single-electrode datasets of monkeys A, B and J and all EMG are not in it.

The positions are stored as numbers in mm with unit meters and conversion 0.001, which is consistent; the derivative of position matches hand_vel with slope about 1, so velocity is in mm/s. Every unit's electrodes entry points to the PMd group, but the unit ids carry two array prefixes (1 and 2) and the electrode index equals the channel number minus one for both, so units of the second array point to PMd electrodes as well. The electrodes table has no positions. Both are findings.

Clock check¶

Spikes and the trial table: decode the side of the reach target (target x > 0) from population spike counts in 100 ms windows around target onset, leave-one-trial-out, nearest class mean on z-scored counts. Before target onset the target is unknown and decoding should be at chance; after it, above chance. The same is shown with the labels of the next trial (a shifted label sequence). Hand and trial table: hand speed around the stored movement onset.

In [3]:
rng_clock = np.random.default_rng(0)

def window_counts(t_ref, w0, w1):
    X = np.zeros((len(trials), len(units)))
    for u, s in enumerate(data["spikes"]):
        lo = np.searchsorted(s, t_ref + w0)
        hi = np.searchsorted(s, t_ref + w1)
        X[:, u] = hi - lo
    return X

def loo_centroid_accuracy(X, y):
    X = (X - X.mean(0)) / (X.std(0) + 1e-9)
    hits = 0
    for i in range(len(y)):
        tr_ = np.arange(len(y)) != i
        m1 = X[tr_ & (y == 1)].mean(0); m0 = X[tr_ & (y == 0)].mean(0)
        pred = int(np.sum((X[i] - m1) ** 2) < np.sum((X[i] - m0) ** 2))
        hits += pred == y[i]
    return hits / len(y)

y_side = (trials.target_x.values > 0).astype(int)
y_next = np.r_[y_side[1:], y_side[:1]]
rows = []
for w0 in np.arange(-0.4, 0.6, 0.1):
    X = window_counts(trials.target_on_time.values, w0, w0 + 0.1)
    rows.append({"window re target onset (ms)": f"{int(round(w0*1000))} to {int(round((w0+0.1)*1000))}",
                 "accuracy, true labels": loo_centroid_accuracy(X, y_side),
                 "accuracy, next trial's labels": loo_centroid_accuracy(X, y_next)})
clock = pd.DataFrame(rows)
null = [loo_centroid_accuracy(window_counts(trials.target_on_time.values, 0.2, 0.3), rng_clock.permutation(y_side)) for _ in range(50)]
print(clock.round(2).to_string(index=False))
print("chance: majority class %.2f; permuted labels at 200 to 300 ms, 95th percentile %.2f" % (max(y_side.mean(), 1 - y_side.mean()), np.percentile(null, 95)))
speed_at = lambda lag: np.array([np.hypot(*beh["vel"][np.searchsorted(beh["t"], t + lag)]) for t in trials.move_onset_time])
s_before, s_on, s_after = speed_at(-0.1), speed_at(0.0), speed_at(0.1)
print("hand speed (mm/s) median at move onset -100 ms %.1f, at onset %.1f, +100 ms %.1f; trials faster at +100 than -100: %d of %d"

Duplicated recordings¶

The test file holds 0.7 s segments with movement onset at 250 ms. Are any of them copies of train trials? Each test segment's spike counts of the held-in units are compared with the counts of every train trial in the window 250 ms before to 450 ms after its movement onset. Train trials are also compared with each other.

Shared computations¶

Condition means under each reading of the open details the claims file names: movement onset (O3a, the dataset's move_onset_time; O3b, hand speed reaching 15% of its trial peak) and the proto-trial filter (O4a, b, c). Only trials with delay > 400 ms are used. A condition is a maze_id and trial_version pair (27). Spike trains are smoothed with a 20 ms Gaussian before averaging (Supplemental Experimental Procedures). The 10 ms time step of the T matrices is O5.

Reliability of condition means¶

The paper's J-array dataset averaged about 20 trials per condition (2166 trials per neuron over 108 conditions); here there are 1 to 4. As a reference for every claim below, the split-half reliability of each unit's preparatory and peri-movement tuning: over the conditions with at least two trials, the correlation between the condition means of one trial (the first) and of the others.

In [6]:
Rg, Rm = RATES["a"]
Pt = mp.epoch_mean(Rg, GO_L, mp.PREP_WIN)       # trials x units
Mt = mp.epoch_mean(Rm, MV_L, mp.PERI_WIN)
multi = [c for c in range(C) if (conds == c).sum() >= 2]
first = np.array([np.flatnonzero(conds == c)[0] for c in multi])
rest_P = np.stack([Pt[np.flatnonzero(conds == c)[1:]].mean(0) for c in multi])
rest_M = np.stack([Mt[np.flatnonzero(conds == c)[1:]].mean(0) for c in multi])
rel_P = mp.rowwise_corr(Pt[first], rest_P)
rel_M = mp.rowwise_corr(Mt[first], rest_M)
pt_main = mp.tuning(CONFIGS[MAIN]["P"], "range")
print("conditions with >= 2 trials:", len(multi))
for name, r in (("preparatory", rel_P), ("peri-movement", rel_M)):
    r = r[np.isfinite(r)]
    print(f"{name} split-half r over units: median {np.median(r):.2f}, IQR {np.percentile(r,25):.2f} to {np.percentile(r,75):.2f}")
sel5 = pt_main > mp.PREP_TUNING_MIN
print("same, units with > 5 spikes/s preparatory range: preparatory median %.2f, peri-movement median %.2f"
      % (np.nanmedian(rel_P[sel5]), np.nanmedian(rel_M[sel5])))
sel_sd = mp.tuning(CONFIGS[MAIN]["P"], "sd") > mp.PREP_TUNING_MIN
print("same, units with > 5 spikes/s preparatory SD (n = %d): preparatory median %.2f (values %s), peri-movement median %.2f"
      % (sel_sd.sum(), np.nanmedian(rel_P[sel_sd]), np.round(np.sort(rel_P[sel_sd]), 2), np.nanmedian(rel_M[sel_sd])))

Readings adopted where readings differ (author, step 1.6)¶

Every claim below is run under every reading the claims file names. Where they give different outcomes, these are adopted as assumptions, and the outcome is marked as resting on them:

  • O1, "spikes/s of preparatory tuning" (Methods, Neural recordings and datasets): the range of the preparatory rate across conditions (O1a). The Methods speak of a rate difference ("Firing rate modulation was typically lower for the array recordings ... We thus used a lower inclusion criterion:

    5 spikes/s of preparatory tuning"), which the range measures directly. The SD reading (O1b) is shown everywhere.

  • O3, movement onset: the dataset's move_onset_time (O3a), computed by the data's authors ("calculated offline using a robust algorithm", its description). The paper defers to Churchland et al. (2006c).
  • O4, the proto-trial: a trial of the condition, the one best correlated with the condition mean (O4a), since the Supplemental Experimental Procedures call it a "reference 'proto-trial'".
  • Units in the peri-movement T matrix ("all neurons except the neuron whose preparatory activity we were trying to capture", Methods): all recorded units (main) and, as a second reading, the units passing the inclusion rule; both are run in fig6d. Under O1a they give the same outcome.

fig4d-mean-correlation-j-array¶

For the J-array dataset, the correlation across conditions between a unit's preparatory and peri-movement firing rates is positive on average but small (mean Pearson r = 0.13, p = 0.03; mean Spearman r = 0.11).

Criterion: units with > 5 spikes/s of preparatory tuning and peri-movement tuning at least 1.5 times as strong, under O1 (range, SD) and O2 (i epoch means, ii largest tuning at any time); O3 and O4 as above; the mean against zero by (a) one-sample t-test, (b) t-test on Fisher z, (c) Wilcoxon. Expected mean Pearson 0.13 ± 0.013 and Spearman 0.11 ± 0.011.

In [7]:
def fig4_units(cfg, O1, O2):
    pt = mp.tuning(cfg["P"], O1)
    qt = mp.peri_tuning(cfg["CMm"], MV_L, cfg["M"], O1, O2)
    return (pt > mp.PREP_TUNING_MIN) & (qt >= mp.PERI_RATIO_MIN * pt)

def fig4_corrs(cfg, sel):
    r = mp.rowwise_corr(cfg["P"][:, sel], cfg["M"][:, sel])
    rs = np.array([stats.spearmanr(cfg["P"][:, j], cfg["M"][:, j])[0] for j in np.flatnonzero(sel)])
    return r, rs

rows = []
for (o, f), cfg in CONFIGS.items():
    for O1 in ("range", "sd"):
        for O2 in ("i", "ii"):
            sel = fig4_units(cfg, O1, O2)
            row = {"O3": o, "O4": f, "O1": O1, "O2": O2, "n units": int(sel.sum())}
            if sel.sum() >= 3:
                r, rs = fig4_corrs(cfg, sel)
                row.update({"mean r": r.mean(), "mean Spearman": rs.mean(),
                            "p t": stats.ttest_1samp(r, 0).pvalue,
                            "p t(z)": stats.ttest_1samp(np.arctanh(np.clip(r, -0.999, 0.999)), 0).pvalue,
                            "p Wilcoxon": stats.wilcoxon(r).pvalue})
                row["within tol"] = abs(r.mean() - 0.13) <= 0.013 and abs(rs.mean() - 0.11) <= 0.011
                row["positive, p<0.05 (any test)"] = r.mean() > 0 and min(row["p t"], row["p t(z)"], row["p Wilcoxon"]) < 0.05
            rows.append(row)
fig4_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(fig4_table.round(3).to_string(index=False))
print("units selected under O1 range / O1 SD (preparatory > 5 spikes/s, main O3/O4):",
      int((mp.tuning(CONFIGS[MAIN]["P"], "range") > 5).sum()), "/", int((mp.tuning(CONFIGS[MAIN]["P"], "sd") > 5).sum()), "of", len(units))
ok = fig4_table.dropna(subset=["mean r"])
print("readings with >= 3 units:", len(ok), "| within tolerance and p < 0.05:",
      int((ok["within tol"] & ok["positive, p<0.05 (any test)"]).sum()),
      "| positive at p < 0.05:", int(ok["positive, p<0.05 (any test)"].sum()))
print("mean r over readings: min %.3f max %.3f; mean Spearman min %.3f max %.3f"
      % (ok["mean r"].min(), ok["mean r"].max(), ok["mean Spearman"].min(), ok["mean Spearman"].max()))
sel_main = fig4_units(CONFIGS[MAIN], "range", "i")
r_main, rs_main = fig4_corrs(CONFIGS[MAIN], sel_main)
print("main reading (O1 range, O2 i, O3a, O4a): n = %d, mean r = %.3f, mean Spearman = %.3f, conditions = %d"
      % (sel_main.sum(), r_main.mean(), rs_main.mean(), C))
for arr in ("PMd", "M1"):
    m = (units.array.values == arr)[sel_main]
    print(f"  {arr} (by unit id prefix): n = {m.sum()}, mean r = {r_main[m].mean():.3f}")
# the units of the widest selection (O2 ii) for reference
sel_ii = fig4_units(CONFIGS[MAIN], "range", "ii")
r_ii, rs_ii = fig4_corrs(CONFIGS[MAIN], sel_ii)
print("O2 ii (main otherwise): n = %d, mean r = %.3f (t-test p = %.3f), mean Spearman %.3f" % (sel_ii.sum(), r_ii.mean(), stats.ttest_1samp(r_ii, 0).pvalue, rs_ii.mean()))

Noise reference for fig4d, fig4-broad-near-zero, fig4e and suppfig1¶

With 1 to 4 trials per condition, the preparatory and peri-movement means of a condition share the noise of the same few trials, and the preparatory window ends 100 ms after the go cue, about 220 ms before movement onset (median reaction time 321 ms). Two references are computed on the main reading (O3a, O4a, O1a):

  • condition-shuffled null: the condition labels of the kept trials are permuted (counts kept), and the whole pipeline (selection, correlations, time course, population averages) is run on the shuffled means, 20 times. There is no tuning in these data, only trial noise.
  • disjoint trials: within each condition with at least two kept trials, alternate trials go to two sets; the preparatory means come from one set and the movement-locked means from the other, both ways. Single-trial conditions are dropped. Units are those of fig4d on all trials. Shared trial noise cannot correlate the two means here.

The time-course and population-average functions used by fig4e and suppfig1 are defined here.

In [8]:
LAGS_MV = np.arange(-400, 401, 10)
LAGS_GO = np.arange(-200, 201, 10)

def time_course(cfg, sel):
    P = cfg["P"][:, sel]
    mv = np.array([np.nanmean(mp.rowwise_corr(P, cfg["CMm"][:, sel, np.flatnonzero(MV_L == t)[0]])) for t in LAGS_MV])
    go = np.array([np.nanmean(mp.rowwise_corr(P, cfg["CMg"][:, sel, np.flatnonzero(GO_L == t)[0]])) for t in LAGS_GO])
    return go, mv

def judge_tc(mv):
    at0 = mv[LAGS_MV == 0][0]; at200 = mv[LAGS_MV == -200][0]
    drops = mv[:-5] - mv[5:]            # drop over 50 ms starting at each lag
    start = LAGS_MV[:-5][np.argmax(drops)]
    return {"r at -200": at200, "r at 0": at0, "largest 50 ms drop starts": start,
            "pass": at0 < 0.1 and at0 < 0.5 * at200 and -300 <= start <= 0,
            "partial": at0 >= 0.1 and at0 < at200}

def pop_avg(cfg, sel, normalise=True):
    P = cfg["P"][:, sel]
    n_c = P.shape[0]
    order = np.argsort(P, axis=0)
    ranks = [order[-1], order[int(round((n_c - 1) * 2 / 3))], order[int(round((n_c - 1) / 3))], order[0]]
    idx = np.flatnonzero(sel)
    go_tr, mv_tr = [], []
    for rk in ranks:
        g = np.stack([cfg["CMg"][c, u] for c, u in zip(rk, idx)])
        m = np.stack([cfg["CMm"][c, u] for c, u in zip(rk, idx)])
        if normalise:
            mx = np.maximum(cfg["CMg"][:, idx].max((0, 2)), cfg["CMm"][:, idx].max((0, 2)))
            g, m = g / mx[:, None], m / mx[:, None]
        go_tr.append(g.mean(0)); mv_tr.append(m.mean(0))
    return np.array(go_tr), np.array(mv_tr)

def judge_pop(go_tr, mv_tr):
    prep = (GO_L >= mp.PREP_WIN[0]) & (GO_L <= mp.PREP_WIN[1])
    spread_prep = (go_tr[0] - go_tr[3])[prep].mean()
    spread_0 = (mv_tr[0] - mv_tr[3])[MV_L == 0][0]
    top150 = mv_tr[:, MV_L == -150][:, 0]
    return {"spread prep": spread_prep, "spread at onset": spread_0, "ratio": spread_0 / spread_prep,
            "strongest on top at -150": bool(np.argmax(top150) == 0),
            "pass": spread_0 < 0.5 * spread_prep and np.argmax(top150) == 0}

def means_from(o, idx_prep, idx_peri, labels, cond_list):
    """Condition means over `cond_list`, go-locked from trials idx_prep and movement-locked from
    idx_peri (positions in `keep`), with the given condition label of every kept trial."""
    Rg, Rm = RATES[o]
    cm = lambda R, idx: np.stack([R[idx[labels[idx] == c]].mean(0) for c in cond_list])
    cfg = {"CMg": cm(Rg, idx_prep), "CMm": cm(Rm, idx_peri)}
    cfg["P"] = mp.epoch_mean(cfg["CMg"], GO_L, mp.PREP_WIN)
    cfg["M"] = mp.epoch_mean(cfg["CMm"], MV_L, mp.PERI_WIN)
    return cfg

def noise_row(cfg, sel=None):
    sel_b = mp.tuning(cfg["P"], "range") > mp.PREP_TUNING_MIN
    sel = fig4_units(cfg, "range", "i") if sel is None else sel
    r, _ = fig4_corrs(cfg, sel)
    q1, q3 = np.nanpercentile(r, [25, 75])
    ja, jb = judge_tc(time_course(cfg, sel)[1]), judge_tc(time_course(cfg, sel_b)[1])
    pa = judge_pop(*pop_avg(cfg, sel, True))
    return {"n > 5 spikes/s": int(sel_b.sum()), "n fig4": int(sel.sum()), "mean r": np.nanmean(r), "IQR r": q3 - q1,
            "fig4e(a) r -200": ja["r at -200"], "r 0": ja["r at 0"], "drop": ja["largest 50 ms drop starts"], "pass (a)": ja["pass"],
            "fig4e(b) r -200": jb["r at -200"], "r 0 (b)": jb["r at 0"], "pass (b)": jb["pass"],
            "suppfig1 ratio": pa["ratio"], "top at -150": pa["strongest on top at -150"], "suppfig1 pass": pa["pass"]}

rng_null = np.random.default_rng(7)
kp_main = np.flatnonzero(CONFIGS[MAIN]["kept"])
rows = [{"set": "data (main reading)", **noise_row(CONFIGS[MAIN])}]
for s in range(20):
    lab = conds.copy(); lab[kp_main] = rng_null.permutation(conds[kp_main])
    rows.append({"set": f"shuffle {s + 1}", **noise_row(means_from("a", kp_main, kp_main, lab, range(C)))})
null_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("condition-shuffled null, main reading")
print(null_table.round(3).to_string(index=False))
nt = null_table.iloc[1:]
print("over 20 shuffles: units passing > 5 spikes/s range %d to %d (data %d of %d); fig4e passes (a) %d, (b) %d; suppfig1 passes %d;"
      % (nt["n > 5 spikes/s"].min(), nt["n > 5 spikes/s"].max(), null_table["n > 5 spikes/s"].iloc[0], len(units),
         nt["pass (a)"].sum(), nt["pass (b)"].sum(), nt["suppfig1 pass"].sum()))
print("  mean r %.3f to %.3f; IQR of r %.3f to %.3f; fig4e(b) r at -200 %.2f to %.2f and at onset %.3f to %.3f"
      % (nt["mean r"].min(), nt["mean r"].max(), nt["IQR r"].min(), nt["IQR r"].max(),
         nt["fig4e(b) r -200"].min(), nt["fig4e(b) r -200"].max(), nt["r 0 (b)"].min(), nt["r 0 (b)"].max()))

rows = []
for key, cfg in CONFIGS.items():
    kp = np.flatnonzero(cfg["kept"])
    A, B, both = [], [], []
    for c in range(C):
        idx = kp[conds[kp] == c]
        if len(idx) >= 2:
            A += list(idx[0::2]); B += list(idx[1::2]); both.append(c)
    A, B = np.array(A), np.array(B)

    for name, (X, Y) in (("prep A, move B", (A, B)), ("prep B, move A", (B, A))):

        rows.append({"O3": key[0], "O4": key[1], "split": name, "conditions": len(both), "trials": f"{len(X)}/{len(Y)}",
                     **noise_row(d, sel[0])})
disj_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).drop(columns=["n > 5 spikes/s"])
print()

      % (disj_table["pass (a)"].sum(), disj_table["pass (b)"].sum(), len(disj_table), disj_table["suppfig1 pass"].sum(),
         disj_table["fig4e(b) r -200"].min(), disj_table["fig4e(b) r -200"].max()))

Noise reference. With condition labels shuffled, 82 to 96 units pass the > 5 spikes/s range rule, against 93 with the true labels: under O1a the selection admits units whose range comes from trial noise. The paper justified the 5 spikes/s threshold by its trial count ("acceptable given the higher signal-to-noise ratio provided by the higher trial count", Methods), which this dandiset does not have. The conclusions of fig4d, fig4-broad-near-zero, fig4e and suppfig1 below refer to both references.

Result: not reproduced. Under none of the 18 readings with units is the mean correlation within 0.13 ± 0.013 or positive at p < 0.05: mean r ranges from -0.148 to 0.095 and mean Spearman r from -0.061 to 0.061 (main reading -0.079 and -0.020, 19 units, 27 conditions); the one reading at p < 0.05 has a negative mean. With condition labels shuffled the mean r is -0.106 to 0.074, so the main value is within what trial noise gives. The condition means here rest on 1 to 4 trials, and their split-half reliability (above) is low, so a weak true correlation such as 0.13 could not be resolved; the outcome is a property of these 100 trials, not a test of the paper's J-array data.

fig4abc-mean-correlation-other-datasets¶

Blocked, data_missing: the dandiset holds no single-electrode recordings of monkeys A, B or J (one subject, Jenkins, two Utah arrays).

fig4-broad-near-zero¶

Correlations between preparatory and peri-movement tuning span a broad range centred near zero, with no separate populations of concordant (r near 1) and opposing (r near -1) tuning; most neurons have weakly correlated tuning.

Criterion: on the units and correlations of fig4d, median r in [-0.3, 0.3], IQR at least 0.3, more than half of units with |r| < 0.5, fewer than 15% above 0.8 and fewer than 15% below -0.8.

In [9]:
def broad(r):
    q1, q3 = np.percentile(r, [25, 75])
    out = {"n": len(r), "median": np.median(r), "IQR": q3 - q1, "frac |r|<0.5": np.mean(np.abs(r) < 0.5),
           "frac r>0.8": np.mean(r > 0.8), "frac r<-0.8": np.mean(r < -0.8)}
    out["pass"] = (-0.3 <= out["median"] <= 0.3 and out["IQR"] >= 0.3 and out["frac |r|<0.5"] > 0.5
                   and out["frac r>0.8"] < 0.15 and out["frac r<-0.8"] < 0.15)
    return out

Result: not reproduced, resting on the assumption that tuning is the range across conditions (O1a). Under O1a (12 readings) the median correlation is near zero (-0.098 to 0.016), 92% to 100% of units have |r| < 0.5, at most 1.2% lie above 0.8 and none below -0.8, but the interquartile range (0.173 to 0.286) is below the 0.3 the criterion asks for a broad range in every O1a reading. The criterion has no partial rule, and the condition that fails is the one that tests the breadth the claim states. The conditions that hold are also met by noise: with condition labels shuffled the IQR is 0.069 to 0.422 and the mean r -0.106 to 0.074. Under O1b (SD; 3 to 5 units) all 6 readings pass.

fig4e-correlation-time-course¶

When peri-movement activity is taken at single time points, its correlation with preparatory tuning starts to fall about 200 ms before movement onset and is near zero by movement onset.

Criterion: the rate at single time points of the 20 ms smoothed condition means, swept along the go-locked and movement-locked means, correlated per unit with the preparatory vector, averaged over units ((a) the fig4 units, (b) all units with > 5 spikes/s preparatory tuning). Reproduced when the mean at movement onset is below 0.1 and below half its value at -200 ms, and the largest drop over a 50 ms step begins between -300 ms and onset.

With the two means taken from disjoint trials, the correlation at -200 ms is only 0.12 to 0.18 for all units, and the criterion is met in 4 of 12 readings (fig4 units) and 9 of 12 (all units). suppfig1-population-averages-lose-tuning¶

Population-average PSTHs grouped by each neuron's preparatory preference show weak peri-movement differences that shrink with time, with little relationship to preparatory tuning by movement onset.

Criterion: per fig4 unit, the conditions with the strongest and weakest preparatory rate and those at the 1/3 and 2/3 ranks; each unit normalised by its maximum rate; averaged. Reproduced when the spread between the strongest and weakest traces at movement onset is less than half the spread in the preparatory epoch, with the strongest still on top at -150 ms. Unnormalised average as a variant.

Result: reproduced; trial noise also meets the criterion in about half the shuffles, so the pass carries little evidence. In all 36 readings (normalised and not) the spread between the strongest and weakest preparatory conditions at movement onset is less than half the preparatory spread (ratio 0.186 in the main normalised reading, -0.175 to 0.295 over readings), with the strongest-preparatory trace on top at 150 ms before onset. With condition labels shuffled the criterion is met in 11 of 20 shuffles. With the preparatory and movement-locked means from disjoint trials it is met in 2 of 12 readings. This suggests that the strongest trace being on top at -150 ms, the part of the result that noise does not give every time, comes mostly from noise shared within the same trials, but it does not show it: each disjoint half uses about half the trials, and the added noise could also hide a real effect.

fig6d-perimovement-best-j-array¶

For the J-array dataset, the cross-validated performance of a preferred direction in capturing preparatory tuning is highest when the PD is expressed in the PCA-based peri-movement space, compared with the kinematic space and the task spaces.

Criterion: units with > 5 spikes/s preparatory tuning (O1); leave-one-condition-out regression on a space plus offset; performance 1 - MSE / variance, averaged over units. Peri-movement space: PC scores of the condition means from -150 to +800 ms of all other units, not normalised. Kinematic space: PC scores of x, y position, velocity and acceleration from -150 ms to the end of the reach (600 or 800 ms), each scaled to unit range; reading (a) repeats the six variables to about n columns and (b) uses them once. The eight maze task spaces of the Methods. k = 1 to 14 and 1 to 20. Reproduced when under each reading the best peri-movement performance over k exceeds the best kinematic one and every task space; partially when it exceeds all but one.

Readings (a) and (b) of the kinematic matrix give the same scores up to a common scale (each variable repeated the same number of times multiplies the Gram matrix by that number), and regression with an offset is unchanged by scaling, so one is computed and the identity is checked below. Segment directions are computed with segments of equal path length and, as a variant, of equal duration.

KMAX = 20
t0 = time.time()

def perf_matrix(P, spaces_per_unit, idx, kmax=KMAX):
    return np.array([mp.loo_performance_curve(P[:, j], spaces_per_unit[j], kmax) for j in idx])

PERF = {}
for key, cfg in CONFIGS.items():
    P = cfg["P"]
    peri = mp.leave_one_out_scores(cfg["CMm"][:, :, TSEL], KMAX)
    upper = mp.leave_one_out_scores(P[:, :, None], KMAX)
    allidx = np.arange(len(units))
    res = {"peri": perf_matrix(P, peri, allidx), "upper": perf_matrix(P, upper, allidx)}
    for end in (600, 800):
        ks = mp.pca_scores(mp.kinematic_matrix(cfg["KIN"], end), KMAX)
        res[f"kin{end}"] = perf_matrix(P, [ks] * len(units), allidx)
    for seg in ("length", "time"):
        for name, S in cfg["TS_" + seg].items():
            res[f"{seg}:{name}"] = np.array([mp.loo_performance(P[:, j], S) for j in allidx])
    res["peri_scores"] = peri
    PERF[key] = res
print(f"performance for all units and readings in {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")

def fig6_summary(key, O1, kmax, end, seg):
    cfg, res = CONFIGS[key], PERF[key]
    sel = mp.tuning(cfg["P"], O1) > mp.PREP_TUNING_MIN
    peri = np.nanmean(res["peri"][sel, :kmax], 0)
    kin = np.nanmean(res[f"kin{end}"][sel, :kmax], 0)
    tasks = {name: np.nanmean(res[f"{seg}:{name}"][sel]) for name in mp.TASK_SPACES}
    return sel, peri, kin, tasks

Spread of the fig6d comparisons, a second reading of the T matrix, and a noise reference.

  • Per reading, the peri-movement performance per unit (at the k best on average) is compared with the best other space per unit by a paired t-test, with SEs across units.
  • The Methods say each row of the T matrix "contained data from all neurons except the neuron whose preparatory activity we were trying to capture", and that "Analysis of preparatory responses was restricted to neurons with at least 10 spikes/s of preparatory tuning" (5 for the arrays). "All neurons" may be all recorded units (main, 142) or the included units only; both are run.
  • Condition-shuffled null (main reading, 10 shuffles): the neural condition labels are permuted, the kinematic and task spaces are left intact, and the same comparison is made.

rows = []
for key in CONFIGS:
    res = PERF[key]
    for O1 in ("range", "sd"):
        sel = mp.tuning(CONFIGS[key]["P"], O1) > mp.PREP_TUNING_MIN
        for kmax in (14, 20):
            for end in (600, 800):
                for seg in ("length", "time"):
                    peri = res["peri"][sel, :kmax]
                    pu = peri[:, np.argmax(np.nanmean(peri, 0))]
                    kin = res[f"kin{end}"][sel, :kmax]
                    others = {"kinematic": kin[:, np.argmax(np.nanmean(kin, 0))],
                              **{name: res[f"{seg}:{name}"][sel] for name in mp.TASK_SPACES}}
                    best_o = max(others, key=lambda k: np.nanmean(others[k]))
                    d = pu - others[best_o]
                    rows.append({"O3": key[0], "O4": key[1], "O1": O1, "kmax": kmax, "kin end": end, "segments": seg,
                                 "peri": np.nanmean(pu), "SE peri": np.nanstd(pu) / np.sqrt(len(pu)), "best other": best_o,
                                 "other": np.nanmean(others[best_o]), "peri - other": np.nanmean(d),
                                 "SE diff": np.nanstd(d) / np.sqrt(len(d)), "p paired t": stats.ttest_rel(pu, others[best_o], nan_policy="omit").pvalue})
f6_tests = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f6_tests.drop_duplicates(subset=["O3", "O4", "O1", "best other", "peri", "other"]).round(3).to_string(index=False))
print("(rows identical in all values but kmax, kin end and segments are shown once)")
print("readings where the peri-movement space is better than the best other space at p < 0.05: %d of %d; p range %.2f to %.2f"
      % (((f6_tests["p paired t"] < 0.05) & (f6_tests["peri - other"] > 0)).sum(), len(f6_tests), f6_tests["p paired t"].min(), f6_tests["p paired t"].max()))

        sc = mp.leave_one_out_scores(cfg["CMm"][:, :, TSEL], KMAX, members=sel)
        pm = np.nanmean(perf_matrix(cfg["P"], sc, np.flatnonzero(sel)), 0)
        kin = np.nanmean(PERF[key]["kin800"][sel], 0).max()
        tasks = {n: np.nanmean(PERF[key][f"length:{n}"][sel]) for n in mp.TASK_SPACES}
        best_t = max(tasks, key=tasks.get)

        rows.append({"O3": key[0], "O4": key[1], "O1": O1, "n": int(sel.sum()),

                     "peri best, T of included units": pm.max(), "k": int(np.argmax(pm) + 1), "kin best": kin,
                     "best task": tasks[best_t], "spaces >= peri (included)": n_beat,
                     "outcome (included)": "reproduced" if n_beat == 0 else ("partial" if n_beat == 1 else "no")})

Result: partially reproduced, resting on the assumption O1a. In the main reading the best peri-movement performance (-0.044 at k = 2) is above the best kinematic (-0.053) and every task space (best, initial velocity, -0.048). Over the 96 readings 64 meet the criterion and 32 are partial: under O1a with the condition mean as proto-trial (O4b), or with the speed-based onset (O3b) and a filter, and under O1b with O3b and O4b, the initial-velocity or kinematic space matches or beats it. The criterion asks that it hold under each reading, so the outcome is partial. The differences are small against their spread: in no reading is the peri-movement space better than the best other space at p < 0.05 (paired t p 0.47 to 0.98; main reading difference 0.004, SE 0.018). With the T matrix built from the included units only, O1a gives the same (reproduced or partial in each of 6 settings), while under O1b the peri-movement space falls to -0.022 to 0.101 and 6 to 8 spaces match or beat it. Under O1a every space performs below zero, worse than predicting the mean rate, but above the condition-shuffled null (peri-movement -0.214 to -0.092, kinematic -0.138 to -0.108), so the data carry some tuning these spaces capture.

fig6-perimovement-best-each-dimensionality¶

Taken one dimensionality at a time, performance is almost always higher in the peri-movement space than in other spaces of the same dimensionality.

                    sel, peri, kin, tasks = fig6_summary(key, O1, kmax, end, seg)
                    wins = total = 0
                    for k in range(1, kmax + 1):

fig6e-summary-rank¶

Blocked, data_missing: Figure 6E combines monkeys A, B and J with EMG spaces, none of which are in the dandiset. As the criterion asks, the same ranking without EMG is shown on the J-array data: for limits 3, 6 and 12, the best PCA-based performance with k up to the limit and each task space at or under it, with SEs across units and paired tests against the best space.

In [17]:
res, sel = PERF[MAIN], mp.tuning(CONFIGS[MAIN]["P"], "range") > 5
for lim in (3, 6, 12):
    vals = {"peri-movement": res["peri"][sel, :lim], "kinematic": res["kin800"][sel, :lim]}
    per_unit = {}
    for name, v in vals.items():
        kb = np.argmax(np.nanmean(v, 0))
        per_unit[name] = v[:, kb]
    for name in mp.TASK_SPACES:
        if dims[name] <= lim:
            per_unit[name] = res[f"length:{name}"][sel]
    means = {k: np.nanmean(v) for k, v in per_unit.items()}
    best = max(means, key=means.get)
    out = []
    for k, v in per_unit.items():
        p_t = stats.ttest_rel(per_unit[best], v, nan_policy="omit").pvalue if k != best else np.nan
        p_w = stats.wilcoxon(per_unit[best], v).pvalue if k != best else np.nan
        out.append({"space": k, "mean": means[k], "SE": np.nanstd(v) / np.sqrt(np.isfinite(v).sum()), "p paired t": p_t, "p Wilcoxon": p_w})
    print(f"limit {lim}: best space {best}")
    print(pd.DataFrame(out).round(4).to_string(index=False))

prep-dimensionality-7-to-10¶

Preparatory activity is moderately high dimensional; depending on the dataset 7 to 10 dimensions capture 90% of its variance.

Criterion: PCA of the c x n matrix of condition-mean preparatory rates of the fig6d units; the number of components reaching 90% of the variance; expected 8.65 ± 2.35 (6.3 to 11). Unnormalised main, z-scored variant; bounded by c - 1 = 26.

fig7a-shuffled-space-poor¶

A control peri-movement space in which each condition's peri-movement response is inverted at random on half the conditions performs poorly.

Criterion: for each unit and condition with probability 0.5 the activity after -150 ms is reflected around the rate at -150 ms; the shuffled T matrix is the space; per condition for all units as a variant; 20 shuffles. Reproduced when the best shuffled performance over k is below half the best intact performance and below the best kinematic performance.

In [19]:
rng_shuf = np.random.default_rng(2)
t0 = time.time()

def shuffled_perf(cfg, sel, mode, rng, kmax=14):
    B = cfg["CMm"][:, :, TSEL].copy()           # c x n x t, first sample is -150 ms
    flip = rng.random((C, len(units))) < 0.5 if mode == "unit" else np.repeat(rng.random((C, 1)) < 0.5, len(units), 1)
    B[flip] = 2 * B[flip][:, :1] - B[flip]
    sc = mp.leave_one_out_scores(B, kmax)
    return np.nanmean(perf_matrix(cfg["P"], sc, np.flatnonzero(sel), kmax), 0)

rows = []
for key in CONFIGS:
    cfg = CONFIGS[key]
    for O1 in ("range", "sd"):
        sel = mp.tuning(cfg["P"], O1) > mp.PREP_TUNING_MIN
        intact = np.nanmean(PERF[key]["peri"][sel, :14], 0).max()
        kin = np.nanmean(PERF[key]["kin800"][sel, :14], 0).max()
        for mode in ("unit", "condition"):
            best = [shuffled_perf(cfg, sel, mode, rng_shuf).max() for _ in range(20)]
            rows.append({"O3": key[0], "O4": key[1], "O1": O1, "coin per": mode, "intact best": intact, "kin best": kin,
                         "shuffled best (mean of 20)": np.mean(best), "min": np.min(best), "max": np.max(best),
                         "pass": np.mean(best) < 0.5 * intact and np.mean(best) < kin})
shuf_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(shuf_table.round(3).to_string(index=False))
print(f"{time.time() - t0:.1f} s")

Result: reproduced, weakly. In all 24 readings (six O3/O4 settings, O1a and O1b, the coin per unit or per condition) the shuffled space's best performance (mean of 20 shuffles) is below half the intact best and below the best kinematic performance: main reading -0.097 against -0.044 intact and -0.053 kinematic. Under O1a the intact space is itself below zero, so "below half the intact best" is met trivially; the evidence is the O1b readings (7 or 8 units), where the shuffled mean is -0.065 to 0.041 against an intact 0.129 to 0.249.

fig7b-window-start-slide¶

Sliding the start of the peri-movement window later costs little; with the window starting at movement onset, performance is still 97% (monkey J) and 94% (monkeys A, B) of its original value.

Criterion: performance averaged across units at the best k for each start time, window end fixed; the J value under reading (a), J-array; expected ratio 0.97 ± 0.097. Monkeys A and B are not in the dandiset.

In [20]:
STARTS = [-150, -100, -50, 0, 50, 100]
rows = []
for key in CONFIGS:
    cfg = CONFIGS[key]
    for O1 in ("range", "sd"):
        sel = mp.tuning(cfg["P"], O1) > mp.PREP_TUNING_MIN
        row = {"O3": key[0], "O4": key[1], "O1": O1}
        for s in STARTS:
            tsel = (MV_L >= s) & (MV_L <= mp.T_WIN[1]) & ((MV_L - s) % mp.STEP_MS == 0)
            sc = mp.leave_one_out_scores(cfg["CMm"][:, :, tsel], 14)
            row[s] = np.nanmean(perf_matrix(cfg["P"], sc, np.flatnonzero(sel), 14), 0).max()
        row["ratio 0/-150"] = row[0] / row[-150] if row[-150] > 0 else np.nan   # a ratio of negative performances is undefined
        rows.append(row)
slide_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)

      "| within 0.97 +/- 0.097:", int(((slide_table["ratio 0/-150"] - 0.97).abs() <= 0.097).sum()))

Result: not reproduced, resting on the SD reading of tuning (O1b), the only reading under which the ratio is defined. Under O1b the ratio of performance with the window starting at movement onset to that at -150 ms is 0.471 to 0.761 in the 6 readings, outside 0.97 ± 0.097. Under O1a (6 readings) performance at -150 ms is below zero (-0.046 to -0.023), so the ratio is undefined; from there it falls to -0.059 to -0.046 at onset. The monkeys A and B value cannot be computed from this dandiset.

Anterior and posterior sites¶

The electrodes table has no positions, and every unit's electrodes entry points to the PMd group. The three claims below use array identity as the only anterior-posterior information: PMd anterior, M1 posterior (Supplemental Figure 3 legend: "the first in caudal PMd ... the second in surface M1"). Which array is which is not in the file: the electrode index of both prefixes points into the PMd group. Prefix 1 is read as PMd only because the PMd group comes first in the electrodes table. Each claim's result is shown under both mappings: the regression r with the arrays swapped (ap-location-no-effect-j-array), the raw performance of each half under each mapping (fig7c), and the outcome under each mapping (prep-activity-more-anterior).

ap-location-no-effect-j-array¶

For J-array, the preparatory to peri-movement tuning correlation does not depend on anterior-posterior recording location (r = 0.20, p = 0.27).

Criterion: a claim of absence; the fig4d correlations regressed on AP location, reproduced when p >= 0.05. With array identity only, the two-group comparison (two-sided t-test) is the variant the criterion names; regression on a 0/1 location is the same test.

In [21]:
rows = []
for (o, f), cfg in CONFIGS.items():
    for O1 in ("range", "sd"):
        for O2 in ("i", "ii"):
            sel = fig4_units(cfg, O1, O2)
            if sel.sum() < 4:
                continue
            r, _ = fig4_corrs(cfg, sel)
            ant = (units.array.values == "PMd")[sel].astype(float)
            if ant.min() == ant.max():
                continue
            lr = stats.linregress(ant, r)
            tt_ = stats.ttest_ind(r[ant == 1], r[ant == 0])
            rows.append({"O3": o, "O4": f, "O1": O1, "O2": O2, "n PMd": int(ant.sum()), "n M1": int((1 - ant).sum()),
                         "mean r PMd": r[ant == 1].mean(), "mean r M1": r[ant == 0].mean(),
                         "regression r": lr.rvalue, "p": lr.pvalue, "t-test p": tt_.pvalue})
ap_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
ap_table["regression r, arrays swapped"] = -ap_table["regression r"]   # the 0/1 location is reversed; p is unchanged
print(ap_table.round(3).to_string(index=False))
print("readings with p >= 0.05:", int((ap_table.p >= 0.05).sum()), "of", len(ap_table), "under either mapping of the arrays")

Result: reproduced, resting on the assumption that array identity gives AP location. In all 17 readings with units in both arrays the tuning correlation does not differ between the two arrays (p 0.538 to 1.000; main reading r = 0.105, p = 0.668, 10 and 9 units), under either mapping of the arrays: swapping them changes only the sign of r. With 19 units and two locations the test has little power.

fig7c-anterior-posterior-performance¶

The peri-movement space captures preparatory tuning at both anterior and posterior sites, with normalised performance slightly better at anterior sites.

Criterion: a 6-D peri-movement space; units split by AP (here by array); performance normalised by its upper limit (the PCA space of the preparatory matrix) and compared with random halves; the space built from the half's units or from all units. Reproduced when both halves reach 70% of the random-half normalised performance and the anterior half is higher.

In [22]:
rng_ap = np.random.default_rng(3)
cfg = CONFIGS[MAIN]; P = cfg["P"]
prep_sel = mp.tuning(P, "range") > mp.PREP_TUNING_MIN

def half_perf(members, space_from, prep_sel=prep_sel):
    """Mean 6-D peri performance and upper limit (best k) over prep-tuned units in `members`."""
    mem_space = members if space_from == "half" else np.ones(len(units), bool)
    sc = mp.leave_one_out_scores(cfg["CMm"][:, :, TSEL], 6, members=mem_space)
    up = mp.leave_one_out_scores(P[:, :, None], 14, members=mem_space)
    idx = np.flatnonzero(members & prep_sel)
    perf6 = np.nanmean([mp.loo_performance(P[:, j], sc[j][:, :6]) for j in idx])
    upper = np.nanmean(perf_matrix(P, up, idx, 14), 0).max()
    return perf6, upper, len(idx)

rows = []
pmd = units.array.values == "PMd"
for space_from in ("half", "all"):
    for lab, mem in (("all units", np.ones(len(units), bool)), ("PMd (anterior)", pmd), ("M1 (posterior)", ~pmd)):
        p6, up, n = half_perf(mem, space_from)
        rows.append({"space from": space_from, "subset": lab, "n tuned": n, "perf k=6": p6, "upper limit": up,
                     "normalised": p6 / up if up > 0 else np.nan})
    rand = []
    for _ in range(20):
        mem = np.zeros(len(units), bool); mem[rng_ap.choice(len(units), pmd.sum(), replace=False)] = True
        p6, up, n = half_perf(mem, space_from)
        rand.append((p6, up))
    rand = np.array(rand)
    rows.append({"space from": space_from, "subset": "random halves (20)", "n tuned": np.nan, "perf k=6": rand[:, 0].mean(),
                 "upper limit": rand[:, 1].mean(), "normalised": np.nan})
sd_sel = mp.tuning(P, "sd") > mp.PREP_TUNING_MIN
for lab, mem in (("all units, O1 SD units", np.ones(len(units), bool)), ("PMd (anterior), O1 SD units", pmd), ("M1 (posterior), O1 SD units", ~pmd)):
    p6, up, n = half_perf(mem, "all", sd_sel)
    rows.append({"space from": "all", "subset": lab, "n tuned": n, "perf k=6": p6, "upper limit": up,
                 "normalised": p6 / up if up > 0 else np.nan})
rand = []
for _ in range(20):
    mem = np.zeros(len(units), bool); mem[rng_ap.choice(len(units), pmd.sum(), replace=False)] = True
    if (mem & sd_sel).sum():
        p6, up, n = half_perf(mem, "all", sd_sel)
        rand.append((p6, up, p6 / up if up > 0 else np.nan))
rand = np.array(rand)
rows.append({"space from": "all", "subset": f"random halves ({len(rand)}), O1 SD units", "n tuned": np.nan, "perf k=6": rand[:, 0].mean(),
             "upper limit": rand[:, 1].mean(), "normalised": np.nanmean(rand[:, 2])})
ap7_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(ap7_table.round(3).to_string(index=False))
print("upper limits <= 0 make the normalisation undefined:", int((ap7_table["upper limit"] <= 0).sum()), "of", len(ap7_table))
for a_lab, b_lab, name in (("PMd (anterior)", "M1 (posterior)", "prefix 1 = PMd"), ("M1 (posterior)", "PMd (anterior)", "arrays swapped (prefix 2 = PMd)")):
    t_ = ap7_table[ap7_table["space from"] == "half"].set_index("subset")["perf k=6"]
    print(f"{name}: raw 6-D performance, anterior {t_[a_lab]:.3f}, posterior {t_[b_lab]:.3f} (space from the half's units)")

Result: blocked (other): the normalised measure the criterion uses does not exist here. Under O1a the upper-limit performance is at or below zero for every subset (-0.019 to -0.097), so performance cannot be normalised by it. The raw 6-D performance is far below zero at both arrays: -1.535 (prefix 1) and -1.087 (prefix 2) with the space from the half's units, -1.454 and -1.293 from all units, against -1.008 and -1.400 for random halves. Under O1b (4 and 4 units) the upper limits are positive (0.145 and 0.184) but the 6-D performance is not (normalised -12.048 and -2.915, random halves -7.282), so a threshold at 70% of the random-half value has no meaning either. Under O1b the upper limit of all 8 units (0.123, fig6d cell) is also below the best peri-movement performance (0.209), so it is not a ceiling. Which half is anterior is also not known: with prefix 1 as PMd the anterior half is lower in raw performance (-1.535 against -1.087), with the arrays swapped it is higher.

prep-activity-more-anterior¶

Preparatory activity is more prevalent at anterior sites.

Criterion: the fraction of units passing > 5 spikes/s preparatory tuning (O1) higher anterior than posterior, two-sided Fisher exact test at p < 0.05; partially when higher without significance.

In [23]:
rows = []
for (o, f), cfg in CONFIGS.items():
    for O1 in ("range", "sd"):
        passed = mp.tuning(cfg["P"], O1) > mp.PREP_TUNING_MIN
        a_ = passed[pmd].sum(); b_ = passed[~pmd].sum()
        p = stats.fisher_exact([[a_, pmd.sum() - a_], [b_, (~pmd).sum() - b_]]).pvalue
        fa, fb = a_ / pmd.sum(), b_ / (~pmd).sum()
        judge = lambda ant, post: "reproduced" if ant > post and p < 0.05 else ("partial" if ant > post else "not reproduced")
        rows.append({"O3": o, "O4": f, "O1": O1, "prefix 1 passing": f"{a_}/{pmd.sum()}", "prefix 2 passing": f"{b_}/{(~pmd).sum()}",
                     "frac prefix 1": fa, "frac prefix 2": fb, "Fisher p": p,
                     "outcome if prefix 1 = PMd": judge(fa, fb), "outcome if prefix 2 = PMd": judge(fb, fa)})
prev_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(prev_table.round(4).to_string(index=False))
print(prev_table.groupby("O1")[["outcome if prefix 1 = PMd", "outcome if prefix 2 = PMd"]].agg(lambda x: x.value_counts().to_dict()))
# the same with a measure less sensitive to noise: preparatory range relative to the condition-shuffled range
cfg = CONFIGS[MAIN]; kp = cfg["kept"]
rng_prev = np.random.default_rng(4)
null_rng = np.stack([np.ptp(mp.condition_means(Pt[kp], rng_prev.permutation(conds[kp]), C), axis=0) for _ in range(200)])
z_tune = (np.ptp(cfg["P"], 0) - null_rng.mean(0)) / null_rng.std(0)
print("preparatory range above the 95th percentile of its condition-shuffled null: PMd %d/%d, M1 %d/%d (Fisher p = %.3g); units with no spikes in the epoch give no z"
      % ((z_tune[pmd] > 1.645).sum(), pmd.sum(), (z_tune[~pmd] > 1.645).sum(), (~pmd).sum(),
         stats.fisher_exact([[(z_tune[pmd] > 1.645).sum(), (z_tune[pmd] <= 1.645).sum()], [(z_tune[~pmd] > 1.645).sum(), (z_tune[~pmd] <= 1.645).sum()]]).pvalue))
print("median preparatory range (spikes/s): PMd %.2f, M1 %.2f; mean rate in the preparatory epoch: PMd %.2f, M1 %.2f"
      % (np.median(np.ptp(cfg["P"], 0)[pmd]), np.median(np.ptp(cfg["P"], 0)[~pmd]), cfg["P"].mean(0)[pmd].mean(), cfg["P"].mean(0)[~pmd].mean()))

With prefix 1 as PMd the anterior fraction is lower, not reproduced in all 12 readings; with prefix 2 as PMd it is higher without significance, partially reproduced in all 12 (Fisher p 0.293 to 1.000). Under O1b 4 of 72 and 4 of 70 pass. Units whose range is above the 95th percentile of its condition-shuffled null are 7 of 72 and 6 of 70, and with condition labels shuffled 82 to 96 units pass the O1a rule (noise reference), so under O1a these counts mostly measure noise.

fig7d-pd-consistency¶

The PD measured on two random sets of 25 conditions is more stable (higher dot product) in the peri-movement space than in the task, kinematic and EMG spaces, for every comparison and every dataset.

Criterion: per unit, 25 conditions drawn with replacement, PD fitted, another 25 drawn, PD refitted; dot product averaged over units; 100 repeats. Maze comparison spaces: endpoints + max. spd. (3-D), segment dirs. (6-D), and the kinematic space at its best k; the peri-movement space at the same dimensionality. The task-space axes have mixed units (mm, mm/s), and the PD's direction depends on their scale, which the paper does not give: raw units and z-scored axes are both run.

In [24]:
rng_pd = np.random.default_rng(5)
rows = []
for key, cfg in CONFIGS.items():
    P = cfg["P"]
    ks_kin = mp.pca_scores(mp.kinematic_matrix(cfg["KIN"], 800), KMAX)
    for O1 in ("range", "sd"):
        sel = np.flatnonzero(mp.tuning(P, O1) > mp.PREP_TUNING_MIN)
        kin_k = int(np.argmax(np.nanmean(PERF[key]["kin800"][sel, :14], 0)) + 1)
        comps = {"endpoints + max. spd.": cfg["TS_length"]["endpoints + max. spd."],
                 "segment dirs.": cfg["TS_length"]["segment dirs."], "kinematic (best k)": ks_kin[:, :kin_k]}
        for name, S in comps.items():
            k = S.shape[1]
            for zs in (False, True):
                c_other = np.nanmean([mp.pd_consistency(P[:, j], S, rng_pd, standardize=zs) for j in sel])
                c_peri = np.nanmean([mp.pd_consistency(P[:, j], PERF[key]["peri_scores"][j][:, :k], rng_pd, standardize=zs) for j in sel])
                rows.append({"O3": key[0], "O4": key[1], "O1": O1, "space": name, "k": k, "z-scored axes": zs, "n units": len(sel),
                             "consistency other": c_other, "consistency peri": c_peri, "peri higher": c_peri > c_other})
pd_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(pd_table.round(3).to_string(index=False))
print("comparisons with peri higher:", int(pd_table["peri higher"].sum()), "of", len(pd_table))
print(pd_table.groupby(["O1", "space"])["peri higher"].agg(["sum", "count"]))

fig8-linear-dynamics-simulation¶

In a simulated two-unit rotational linear system with 25 random initial states, the single-unit correlation between initial (preparatory) and later (peri-movement) activity is near zero (0.08), yet a PD in the PCA-based peri-movement space captures the initial state perfectly.

Criterion: x(t+1) = W x(t), W = [1, -2pi/360; 2pi/360, 1], 25 random initial states, 1000 simulations with initial states uniform in the unit disk and in a square, a released interval of 360 steps; reproduced when the median |r| (unit 1 initial rate against its mean over the interval) is below 0.3 and the PD in the 2-D PCA space of the released trajectories gives cross-validated performance above 0.99. The expected value 0.08 ± 0.3 is compared with the median r.

In [25]:
rng_sim = np.random.default_rng(6)
rows = []
for init in ("disk", "square"):
    rs, perfs = [], []
    for _ in range(1000):
        x0, traj = mp.simulate_rotation(rng_sim, init=init)
        later = traj[:, :, 0].mean(1)
        rs.append(np.corrcoef(x0[:, 0], later)[0, 1])
        T = traj.reshape(25, -1)
        perfs.append(mp.loo_performance(x0[:, 0], mp.pca_scores(T, 2)))
    rs, perfs = np.array(rs), np.array(perfs)
    rows.append({"initial states": init, "median r": np.median(rs), "median |r|": np.median(np.abs(rs)),
                 "5th pct r": np.percentile(rs, 5), "95th pct r": np.percentile(rs, 95),
                 "min PD performance": perfs.min(), "median PD performance": np.median(perfs)})
sim_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(sim_table.round(4).to_string(index=False))

initial states  median r  median |r|  5th pct r  95th pct r  min PD performance  median PD performance
          disk    0.0044      0.1114    -0.2533      0.2718                 1.0                    1.0
        square    0.0115      0.1473    -0.3312      0.3304                 1.0                    1.0

Result: reproduced. Over 1000 simulations the median correlation between unit 1's initial rate and its mean over the 360-step released interval is 0.004 (initial states in the unit disk) and 0.012 (in a square), within 0.08 ± 0.3; the median |r| is 0.111 and 0.147, below 0.3; the 2-D PCA-space PD gives leave-one-out performance of 1.0 in every simulation (minimum 1.0).

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The dandiset holds 27 maze conditions with 1 to 4 trials each after the delay rule (78 trials), where the paper's J-array dataset has 108 conditions and about 2166 trials per neuron. Condition means are therefore noisy (median split-half reliability of preparatory tuning 0.20): with condition labels shuffled, about as many units pass the > 5 spikes/s range rule as with the true labels, and the fig4e and suppfig1 criteria are met by trial noise. Under the range reading of tuning every PD space performs below zero, though above a shuffled-label null. Several outcomes differ between the range and SD readings of "spikes/s of tuning"; the SD reading keeps 7 or 8 units, whose preparatory tuning is more reliable over trials (main reading, split-half r median 0.57 against 0.20 over all units, though the units are selected on the same trials). On them every space performs above zero, and the peri-movement space built from all recorded units has the highest mean performance in 5 of the 6 O3/O4 settings (with O3b and O4b the kinematic space is higher, 0.134 against 0.129), but no difference from the best other space is significant (paired t p 0.47 to 0.98); built from those 7 or 8 units only, it is beaten by 6 to 8 spaces. The anterior-posterior claims use array identity, as the electrodes have no positions, and the file does not say which array is PMd. Task-space details the Methods leave open (end of reach, segments, signed peak velocity) are stated in maze_prep.py.

What was found about the dataset.

  • Every unit's electrodes entry points to the PMd electrode group, though unit ids carry two array prefixes (72 units with 1, 70 with 2) and the dataset describes recordings from M1 and PMd; no unit points to an M1 electrode, and nothing in the file says which prefix is PMd.
  • The electrodes table has no positions (x, y, z and impedance are NaN), so no unit has an anterior-posterior location.
  • The dandiset holds one session of the J-array kind, 100 trials of 27 conditions; the single-electrode datasets of monkeys A, B and J, the EMG and 81 of the 108 conditions are not in it, and which trials and conditions were chosen is not said beyond "limited to 100 train trials and 100 test trials".
  • The 100 test segments carry no condition, go cue or behaviour and only the 107 held-in units, so the paper's condition-wise analyses cannot use them; none duplicates a train trial.
  • 22 of the 100 train trials have delays of 400 ms or less, which the paper excludes.
